title: Why reflect on death
hookLine: everyone knows the battery runs out; the Buddha says remembering death leads to the deathless
tomorrow: one more day to practice, or one more breath: which did he praise?

lines: WHY THINK ABOUT IT ON PURPOSE?
cards: Everyone knows they'll die, the way everyone knows a phone battery runs out: in theory, and never while it's at eighty percent. So why think about it on purpose? The Buddha's answer comes with a strange twist.
He says that remembering death, practiced well, plunges into the deathless and ends in the deathless. Thinking about death leads to no-death? That's today's puzzle.

teach.b: The line opens a sutta in the Anguttara Nikaya. Mindfulness of death, developed and practiced often, the Buddha says, brings great fruit and great benefit; it plunges into the deathless.
The Pali for deathless is amata, and here it doesn't mean living forever in this body.
It's a name for nibbana, the peace the Buddha taught as beyond birth and death. So how does remembering death point there? Start with the eighty-percent feeling.
While the battery seems full, everything can wait: the apology, the practice, the call to a grandparent.
Remembering death drains that fake charge. Priorities sort themselves. A grudge looks small.
Kindness looks urgent. And underneath, something loosens: the grip on things that were never going to stay. That loosening, letting go, is the road the Buddha says leads to the deathless.
In the Theravada world, the Visuddhimagga, a classic meditation manual, gives mindfulness of death a long section of its own.
In Tibet, it's the opening of the path, through a teaching handed down from Atisha that the next days will open.
In Zen halls, a wooden board struck before sitting often carries a verse: birth and death are a great matter; impermanence is swift. Different schools, one move. The aim isn't fear.
It's waking up while the battery still has charge, to live well.

how: Reflection on death is taught across Buddhist schools: as one of the recollections in Theravada meditation, as the opening contemplation of the Tibetan lamrim, and in Zen through verses on birth and death; teachers usually pair it with calm and kindness rather than fear.

games.q: what does “why reflect on death” mean?
o: remembering death so you live with clear priorities
a way of making peace with fear by avoiding it
a ritual for calling back the spirits of the dead

games.q: the puzzle, solved — tap the pairs.
p: the deathless, a name for nibbana
birth and death are a great matter

s: Buddhists reflect on death because they see life as gloomy
the aim isn't fear; it's waking up to live well, and the sutta calls it of great benefit.
in the sutta, the deathless means living forever in this body
amata is a name for nibbana, the peace beyond birth and death.
Theravada, Tibetan and Zen practice all make room for remembering death
the Visuddhimagga, the teaching from Atisha, and the Zen board's verse.

games.q: your friend keeps putting off calling her grandfather: 'there's always next weekend.' which reading of today's sutta fits?
o: remembering death drains the 'always next weekend' feeling, so the call matters now.
thinking about death is morbid; better to keep things light with her.
the deathless means there's no rush; everything continues anyway.
games.why: the eighty-percent feeling lets everything wait. remembering death sorts priorities and turns a life toward what matters.

practice: Close your eyes or lower them, and let one quiet sentence rest in the mind: this life will end, and today is part of it. If fear comes, let it be there, and come back to the breath.
If thoughts of death feel heavy or unsafe for you right now, skip this and reach out to someone; in the US you can call or text 988.

wordCard.voice: Why reflect on death: because remembering it drains the fake charge, loosens the grip, and turns a life toward what matters.

orig.note: Pali: maranassati, mindfulness of death, from marana (death) and sati (mindfulness).

carryVoice: For the road: remember death, to live well, while the battery still has charge. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.19 (Maranassati Sutta, opening: mindfulness of death, developed and pursued, is of great fruit and benefit, plunging into and ending in the deathless)
Visuddhimagga, chapter 8 (mindfulness of death among the recollections)
the verse on the Zen han (wooden sounding board): birth and death are a great matter; impermanence is swift
